a742536a-039e-42fe-a7f6-a10184929883.description: Located at an abandoned airport in Iceland, the project explores a playful relationship between architecture and nature through three birdwatching pavilions loosely resembling a fox, a whale, and a bird. Conceived as “clumsy imitators,” the structures respond to the meeting of earth, water, and sky, forming a series of gently awkward shelters along the abandoned runway. Rather than blending seamlessly into their surroundings, they celebrate their imperfect resemblance, inviting visitors to pause, explore, and rediscover the lagoon’s wildlife and landscape with childlike curiosity.

bed1c6b0-b7df-43c9-ad9b-73f1d05d59c0.description:
In September 2026, we were invited to participate in an exhibition at the West Bund Museum. For this exhibition, we explored what it is like to live with trees, and what this relationship means for contemporary life.

The trees sit in planters supported by cantilevered beams and extend through a translucent skin. Watering, pruning, and sweeping up leaves must therefore happen within the residents’ own reach. This constraint—being “within reach”—in turn determines the height of the planters, the position of operable windows, and the depth of the semi-outdoor rooms. Once these activities become part of the home, they introduce a non-negotiable rhythm into daily life. Almost nothing in contemporary life has to happen at a particular moment: work can be postponed, meetings rescheduled, and things bought at any time. Yet in this house, the one thing that cannot be put off is watering. This loss of freedom is voluntarily introduced. It is not a burden, but an anchor.

At the same time, a tree is the only thing in the home that becomes better than it was when you bought it. It moves more slowly than adults, and grows no faster than children. Ten years later, it stands taller than its residents—not because of the design, but because someone has watered it for ten years. Here, then, the relationship between “humans and nature” is not about personifying a tree as a friend. It is about making room for something whose needs are not entirely our own, and accepting the trouble it brings: leaves will fall, branches will grow across windows, and insects will come.

The conclusion is a statement of intent: trouble is not evidence of design failure; it is evidence of design intention. A house without trouble is a house that has never made room for anything other than people.

3fabe620-6eff-418c-9764-a79f7147f71f.description: Located in the agricultural landscape between Dardara and Khiam in South Lebanon, the project uses water-system restoration to address ecological damage, degraded farmland, and displacement caused by conflict. Restored channels, constructed wetlands, and retention basins transform existing wastewater infrastructure into a regenerative landscape supporting irrigation, wildlife habitats, and public life. A continuous walking route connects springs, fields, orchards, and villages, while resting pavilions built from materials recovered from damaged buildings support the gradual renewal of the land, everyday life, and residents’ return.

7049d619-54d3-4971-a8a9-438790f60c0c.description: Located at the foot of the Great Wall in Gubeikou, the project draws on local temple traditions and uses the theme of wishes to connect temples, lanes, and courtyards into public spaces for leisure, social interaction, and markets. Reinterpreting the traditional temple fair for contemporary everyday life, the design introduces a wish-themed market, camping and relaxation areas, and a wish tower. Easy-to-assemble, reusable scaffolding and modular elements accommodate a range of activities, bringing renewed life to the historic street.

472d1c39-1118-4f38-8e4a-dffa0ace25d2.description:
This project treats light as a lived, seasonal condition, shaped not only by apertures and surfaces, but also by the building’s ability to tune its own microclimate throughout the year.

A translucent polycarbonate envelope wraps the three-story timber structure, forming an intermediate thermal buffer that blurs the boundary between interior and exterior while expanding the possibilities of indoor–outdoor living. The house is continuously filled with soft, diffuse daylight. In winter, the envelope captures solar heat gain to reduce heating demand; in summer, operable vents within the skin enable stack-assisted cross-ventilation, flushing excess heat and reducing cooling loads.

Planters project beyond the polycarbonate layer, extending vegetation into the façade itself. Dense summer foliage casts deep shade, while winter leaf drop reopens the house to daylight and warmth, recalibrating comfort across seasons. Each level is paired with a dedicated semi-outdoor room, and selective double-height voids strengthen vertical air movement while intensifying the experience of top light, especially along the circulation core. This vertical illumination is balanced by soft, north-facing diffuse light throughout the interior.

Along the street edge, perforated metal sliding doors fine-tune privacy and porosity, increasing airflow and improving ground-level ventilation. To live here is to inhabit a private forest: plants operate as both architectural skin and optical medium, allowing interior light to grow, filter, and transform over time. A ground-floor courtyard accommodates a reserved parking bay, integrating daily utility without compromising the project’s climatic and atmospheric ambition.

f226b632-3e0c-4e63-b41f-aad5ac72dcfe.description:
On a two-hundred-square-meter site, a single tree is the true center of the
house. The building runs along the western boundary, forming a south-facing
courtyard. The massing is quiet: pitched roofs lean inward, and in section the
volume reads like an inverted trapezoid — rooms gathering toward the trunk,
then rising together. Roof openings are sized against the tree's future crown,
choreographing light, ventilation, and view around its slow becoming. As the
house settles, the sapling grows into the architecture — branches approaching
rooflines, shadows shifting with the seasons, rooms quietly redrawn by time.
Residential House, Osaka

9a6b81da-90e5-4415-99f3-04d63df320d8.description:
When Is Architecture Indestructible? 
Chapter One: Space Nomadism
Architecture has never been truly indestructible.

It has always existed in a dynamic state of tension: between softness and solidity, between movement and permanence. This thesis begins with that false proposition and asks why architecture has gradually moved toward forms associated with strength, durability, and eternity. The answer lies not within architecture itself, but in the social structures and modes of production that shape it.

Historically, the architectures of nomadic civilizations—felt tents, temporary shelters, and foldable framed dwellings—suggest another possibility: architecture does not have to be fixed. It can be soft, reversible, and born through movement with its environment. As Sigfried Giedion argues in Space, Time and Architecture, the evolution of architecture is inseparable from changes in social life and technological development. If society is reconfigured, architectural logic must change with it.

This thesis imagines a speculative future:

Humans become space nomads. The institutions and production systems of Earth no longer exist, and architecture returns to a logic of softness and adaptability. This time, the “tent” is composed of countless inflatable modules that can be assembled, replaced, and grown over time. In a vacuum environment, even a small amount of gas can rapidly expand into a habitable enclosure. When damaged, these modules can be repaired or replaced like cells.

Architecture is no longer a fixed object, but a living process. As Peter Sloterdijk describes in his Spheres trilogy, architecture becomes a “climatic bubble”: a breathable and expandable environment that humans create for survival in the universe.

This project resonates with several existing theoretical lineages:

Softness and reversibility
It echoes Archigram’s 1960s visions of Instant City and Plug-in City, in which architecture is imagined as a temporary structure that can change according to need, rather than as an immovable monument.

Modularity and growth
It extends the thinking of the Japanese Metabolists, who imagined architecture as cellular: capable of replacement, expansion, and repair in response to uncertain populations and environments.

Transparency and immersion
The inflatable membrane blurs the boundary between inside and outside, responding to Sloterdijk’s idea of the “bubble”: humans live within self-generated microclimates, rather than behind rigid and permanent walls.

6d8cc004-10a1-4287-a29c-e7917569bc5e.description:
When Is Architecture Indestructible? 
Chapter Two: Air Dolmen
Transcribing the permanence of megaliths into portable, assemblable, inflatable modularity. When the monument becomes light and soft.

A dolmen is a prehistoric megalithic structure, typically composed of two or more upright stones supporting a massive capstone. Commonly found from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age, dolmens are often associated with burial rituals or ceremonial practices. They represent one of architecture’s earliest forms of permanence, rootedness, and monumentality.

In this thesis, the dolmen is deconstructed and reconstructed through a system of modular inflatable units.

Instead of the mass of stone, Air Dolmen uses the pressure of air. Instead of irreversible heaviness, it relies on replaceable and expandable components.

Monumentality is therefore transformed: from the endurance of stone to the maintenance of a process. Damaged air cushions can be replaced like cells. Structural stiffness is regulated through pressure gradients. A translucent membrane turns the boundary between interior and exterior into a perceptible microclimatic interface, while color-changing liquid within the modules uses evaporation and light scattering to modestly adjust temperature.

Air Dolmen preserves the structural logic of the dolmen, but redefines its monumentality as temporary, soft, and adaptive.

It is a breathing, repairable, and portable monument. As society shifts from settlement toward mobility, and from centralized systems toward distributed networks, architecture no longer proves itself through the eternity of stone. Instead, it extends its meaning through relationships, maintenance, and continuous renewal.

fa1acd49-341e-439f-bb6c-ccb9c0f519c5.description:
A residential intervention in Suzhou's historic district, inserting a classical
garden experience into a modest existing unit. Working within tight budget
constraints, we sourced reclaimed golden floor bricks and salvaged timber
from demolished local buildings — materials that carry the texture of time
without the cost of new. The project resists the impulse to replicate the
garden as spectacle, aiming instead for something quieter: a space where the
sensibility of the Suzhou garden tradition continues to exist, at a domestic
scale, for the people who actually live there.
fa1acd49-341e-439f-bb6c-ccb9c0f519c5.team: RUOQI JIANG, YIBO LIN, MEIHUI WEN

72f15906-8831-48dc-879c-03c3a46197a8.team: MEIHUI WEN, YIBO LIN, RUOQI JIANG

6f956c50-cf1d-4cda-8729-108e0170fd89.description:
The Living Blanket is sited at Plaza Manuel Tolsá in the historic centre of Mexico City, operating under a single concept: patching softness onto rigid urban land.
Constructed from recycled waterproof tarp on a lightweight frame, it collects rainwater to form a shallow reflecting surface and deploys sandbags as anchors, urban furniture, and planters — growing an inhabitable gathering space from the hard ground of a plaza long shaped by colonial and institutional power.
More than shelter, Manta Viva is an act of spatial reclamation: restoring the memory of the land, and returning the ground to those who inhabit it.

180af782-d585-4d51-8ab2-72b91ae97127.description:
The Zigzag Market is a three-story semi-outdoor market structure in San Francisco, CA. The site of the project is the corner of Tennessee St and 22nd St in the Dogpatch neighborhood. The Dogpatch is located near the shoreline of the Bay and straddles a border between residential neighborhoods and a light industrial area. The concept is from analysis of ancient precedent and combine it with ramp circulation of parking-lot. Agora was a central public space in ancient Greek, which consists of stoas, and they can be understood as scattered bars with interactions among them. The concept is rearranging those bars along the continuous ramp system distilled from parking-lot. Just like bars scattered in 3D, they can have interactions with each other in space. Multiple activities can happen in the plaza on the ground floor that opens to the streets. Partially, commercial activities can happen in the spaces with slope to achieve the concept of changing eye-sight and adventurous experience in urban life. To allow people inside to explore inconvenient enjoyment.

For the program on the ground floor, it will be multifunctional and with flexibility for citizens. Exhibitions, flea markets, and neo-retails can take place in the spaces that can open up and turn into semi-outdoor. The plaza, where people can have a sitscually on the stairs, will be a place for performances or public concerts. Semi-outdoor courtyards, where leisure, dining, and having coffee can take place, are spaces in between two stoa bars. Retail stores are mainly on the second floor. And the catering and library are on the third floor. The Roof floor is a greening park. The building will be constructed with steel structure with metal mesh as its elevation surfaces. The whole building is conveying the concept of light, transparent and temporary. Just like Anto Tadao said, architecture is an endless challenge that human beings fight against fateful destruction. So the building aims not to be monumental permanent, but to be something adventurous and ephemeral.

fe8c2eb2-62d8-4d6c-9df1-41564f578ac6.description:
This proposal for Mobile Schools in Palestine explores how a lightweight, adaptable construction system can provide resilient educational spaces within unstable and changing conditions. Using a limited palette of materials, the project transforms basic scaffolding into an expressive and highly flexible architectural framework. Rather than relying on heavy or permanent construction, it proposes a system that can be assembled, modified, relocated, and personalized according to local needs.

The design stands out for its originality and structural clarity. Its construction logic remains simple and accessible, aligning with the skills and techniques familiar to local Palestinian workers. This makes the project not only visually compelling, but also feasible, sustainable, and grounded in the realities of its context.

Flexibility is central to the proposal. The lightweight framework allows for multiple spatial configurations, supporting different scales of learning, gathering, and play. Its adaptable nature gives communities the ability to reshape the school over time, turning the building into a participatory and evolving environment.

Although the project raises questions about impermanence, this temporary quality also becomes one of its strengths. In a context where resilience, mobility, and rapid deployment are essential, the school’s ability to change, move, and be rebuilt offers a meaningful alternative to conventional fixed infrastructure. It is a thoughtful design that balances sustainability, accessibility, and architectural imagination.
fe8c2eb2-62d8-4d6c-9df1-41564f578ac6.team: RUOQI JIANG, SHIMIN ZHOU, YIBO LIN, CHRISSIE CHEN

14906624-562b-4edf-9314-06b8d805e83a.description:
The Lake Chapel of San Giovanni in Val di Lago is a small octagonal church, built in the middle of the sixteenth century on the shores of Bolsena lake, on the ruins of an ancient medieval church, along the Via Francigena.

The Via Francigena is an ancient road and pilgrimage route running from Canterbury in England, through France and Switzerland, to Rome and to Apulia, in southern Italy, where there was the embarkation for the Holy Land. Nowadays many pilgrims still follow this route on foot, on horseback, or by bicycle, as the Via Francigena has been designated Major Cultural Route of the Council of Europe.

This project is aimed to reuse this space as a Pilgrim Center and bring life back inside a late Renaissance church along the Via Francigena path. The design proposal is trying to maximize the appreciation to the chapel and minimize the impacts from the newly added building. Since ruin itself has its unique vitality and beauty that needs to be cherished.

The ruin is close to the sightseeing spots of Lake Bolsena, and it’s located in an idyllic context with flat topography. Meanwhile, the octagonal and symmetrical form of the chapel gives it some properties of centrality and exclusiveness. An attitude of being respectful to this decided that the new building will act as a medium to strengthen the connection between the ruin and its surrounding environment. And in this way, to highlight the chapel’s existence, the new building only serves as its foil. The idea of landscape architecture is largely applied to the external auditorium with a topographic roof connecting to the ground, which allows visitors to walk onto it to have a better and different observation perspective of the ruin. Also, the topographic roof provides natural changes of vegetation throughout the four seasons. To provide visitors with a better view of the lake, a viewing platform is mounted on the top of the dome. And with tree pits installed, it again reflects the landscape architecture.

To minimize the structural impacts to the chapel and according to the octagon shape, eight prefabricated concrete modules are utilized to form the dome. It generates scenes and experiences of the Holy Spirit, which mainly come from the light cast down from the skylight. Artificial light compensation will be used to ensure the light affects all day long. All the modulars are fixed to the foundation and have no structural connection to the ruin wall. It makes the space underneath the dome with opportunities to interact with the outdoor surroundings. On the top of each modular, there is an accommodation with a view looking through the aperture of the old wall.

The space of the auditorium is organized to give it flexibility, which can be switched between indoor & outdoor, large open space & smaller enclosed space. The folding door allows the space to be easily rearranged for different events and have multiple shared space and relationships with its adjacent rooms. And the roof provides a cozy place between the ruin and the auditorium lobby which protects from strong sunshine in the afternoon and allows outdoor events. More pilgrim accommodations are located on the south side of the new building to provide convenience to the visitors who do not want to climb up to the top of the dome and to address the shortage of accommodations in certain periods. For events such as weddings and celebrations, the common dining hall and the auditorium can be used as a whole connected with the transitional space which enhances the interaction with the outdoors and the back side of the chapel. The flexibility provides more opportunities for the site to be used by local communities.

76f4b4dc-9387-431f-8fa9-f8965c18b4bb.description:
The fragmentation between city, architecture, and environment is often a comprehensive reflection of uneven regional development under different historical conditions, as well as cultural perception gaps between generations. This fragmentation is particularly evident in Dessau — a city that experienced rapid expansion before World War II, large-scale destruction during the war, rapid post-war recovery, and later industrial decline after German reunification. In recent decades, the influx of immigrants and the outflow of local residents have further intensified this fragmentation. Based on Landscape Urbanism and the “Green Archipelago” city concept proposed by Ingels, this design uses architecture’s role in urban planning and its dialogue with the surrounding environment to bridge the gap between new and old buildings, younger and older populations, and the city and natural landscape.

Dessau is famous for the Bauhaus. Six Bauhaus craft–themed complexes integrating production, exhibition, civic activity, and leisure will be distributed along the city’s planned tourism ring route. This project is one of them, focusing on the local traditional glass workshop industry. The project is located in front of the old train station — one of the few preserved historical buildings in Dessau — and also along a primary commuting route for younger residents. The site connects to the city’s main transportation hub through a bridge underpass.

The second-floor exhibition space resembles a floating box. The façade is composed of red bricks derived from surrounding historic buildings and frosted glass bricks, organically arranged through parametric methods, creating a visual dialogue between the new and existing architecture.

The ground floor contains two transparent glass boxes and the gray transitional space between them. The northern box functions as a restaurant and bar, with a central corridor reinforcing the entrance to the original office building. This will become a gathering space for people of different age groups.

The southern box serves as a glass craft demonstration space, showcasing the city’s cultural identity to visitors. The central gray space frames the eastern landscape plaza, allowing pedestrians arriving from the new train station to focus on the natural scenery behind the building after passing through the bridge underpass. This semi-outdoor space also supports community public activities. The main glass craft production and storage areas are located underground to accommodate and conceal large machinery. Visual connections between the three floors are created through skylights and glass floor elements. The floor plan composition extracts Suprematist compositional elements from Malevich, including spatial voids, openings, and display furniture layouts. Unlike typical exhibition spaces, because glass crafts are the primary exhibits, skylights on the second floor introduce natural light and create dynamic lighting effects.

bd68dbe1-1b91-4dc3-bc48-c798c2915533.description:
The Rock House is a “Neighborhood Meeting Structure” on a single lot in the middle of a residential block in the middle of a neighborhood in the middle of the San Francisco Bay Area. The concept is from two “structural” precedents, the Dolmen and Dom-Ino, the combination of which contains a series of informal analysis. Eventually, the structure tries to build ambiguity between regularity & irregularity, solidness & void, enclosure & openness, exterior & interior.

“Meeting” as a socially generic problem will be reconsidered spatially in this project. The space of meeting is trying to find a balance between fixed & flexible, private & public, certain & unpredictable.

Through the orthogonal projection operation, irregular stones are turned into L-shaped modules, which will be distributed into the grid system of Dom-Ino. Different combinations of L-shapes can generate various spaces and interactions among them. The operation of cutting is distilled from the Dolmen, which can generate gaps and subtle touches between walls and the ceiling.

The material of the building will be terrazzo, which can ensure that the surface of the interior and the exterior is the same. On one hand, terrazzo possesses the property of stone that it can resist outdoor natural conditions, on the other hand, the smooth surface provides a feeling of intimacy inside. When masonry solidness encounters natural material furniture such as wood and clay, the primitive beauty of materials are emphasized. It aims to create experiences of wabi-sabi. And the irregular geometric form through cutting will allow light to perform differently on the exterior and interior within a day. The tone of terrazzo reflects the warm sunlight of the Bay Area and will react with the artificial light from inside at night.

382dc67a-6889-47fb-abb7-192438971d68.description:
Silver Prize Winner of the Kaira Looro International Architecture Competition, with a nomination recognition from Kengo Kuma.

Our proposal for a Children’s House, called Nest, first and foremost addresses the need for a functional center for medical treatment by creating a simple-to-build, thermally comfortable, and spatially generous place for mothers and children to receive care and grow in health and strength. An inner courtyard is a space for recreation, where children and their families can easily access a place for leisure and relaxation. A strawbale roof & façade envelopes the entire structure, protecting little ones from extreme weather conditions year-round.

Nest’s second responsibility is to show the community the impact of these services and what healing from malnutrition really looks like, as a means of communicating the importance of proper diet and nutrition and the good it can do to children and their families. The administration / educational classroom component sits across from the hospitality area, connected by the inner courtyard. Simple pivoting partitions provide a soft division between these spaces – allowing for some flexibility in privacy as needed from both areas.

It is in the architecture of such a space that the capacity lies to serve as both a practical and educational means of care for the larger community, in service of both treating those in need of care and educating others about how malnutrition can be prevented and what the image of care can be.

488ae7e7-9a56-47de-855c-aa1104369b79.description:
The basis for adaptive reuse more often than not, are actually non-romantic relics from the past. These remnants nevertheless pose important questions in terms of sustainability and construction waste management, as well as deeper philosophical questions regarding originality and authorship. In our confrontation with this set of issues, we refer to Svetlana Boym, who suggests "off-modern" relationships between preservation and development, advocating for designers to engage with traces of the past - past authors, builders, failed projects, and revealing the traces of non-realized compositions. Referencing the concept of pentimenti, "defined in art history as a presence of traces of previous work"

Multi-Sensory Experience: Our proposal is to let the community and nature take back their space to create a place where people are gathered and connected by sharing food and culture. a culinary school serves as an attraction and culture exchange while creating job opportunities, urban living and hospitality weave together to create at the same fabric of the streets of Chinatown inside the building vertically; edible garden as landscape covers the park, crawls over the bridge, flow into the tower and climb up the sky, linking a serious of gardens to become a whole public park.

Yan Huo Qi: A Chinese word literally translated as the smoke, flames and steam, depicts the multi-sensory delight of cooking - the hustle and bustle in mundane life - a healing atmosphere for the nostalgic soul - a sensorial experience that brings back memory despite the irreversibility of time.

TEAM: CHRISSIE

25cbd569-1f58-48f2-b5eb-0caed8f63852.description:
The mid-density multi-family housing project aspires to reshape the Oakland cityscape by creating a dialogue between domestic lives and streets. The architecture's elevation becomes a scroll painting, and the aperture becomes the canvas where the dwellers create their own narrative. By framing domestic life with the windows facing Broadway - the artery of Downtown Oakland, the citizens are the curators of the city.

Elevation as a generator: The city is primarily read and experienced in the “space between the building fronts” as Walter Benjamin calls it. This project investigates the concepts of regulation, ownership, and architectural form through the lens of the relationship between housing and the streets. It explores the potential of the “building front”.

This project investigates the concepts of regulation, ownership, and architectural form through the lens of the relationship between housing and the streets. It explores the potential of the “building front” as a catalyst in creating a relevant contemporary model for large-scale housing and a new urban commons in Oakland. The architectural elevations serve as a device to generate new relationships among urban form, boundaries, density, and legibility. It is no longer just a space divider, but a generator of connection, communication, meaning, shared spaces, and environment stewardship.

TEAM: CHRISSIE CHEN

32042b1b-673d-42ce-93a0-728af877df55.description:
Up Down Space is a public project in Zhangjiang, Shanghai, near a science and technology park. Organized around a hexagonal layout, it aims to create a continuous, engaging environment for different public activities. It includes a large open area for social gathering, a more intimate zone for public art, and a shifting pathway that offers changing views and experiences. Compared with a rectangular plan, the hexagonal geometry provides more flexible routes and multiple axes of movement.

A sunken plaza leads into a multi-purpose public space for speeches, street performances, and community events. A separate, quieter area is reserved for art exhibitions. The underground gallery is reached through a glazed-ceiling passage near the exit, bringing daylight in and maintaining a visual connection to the outdoors. After exploring below ground, visitors follow a twisting ramp up to the roof, enjoying panoramic views along the way. The sequence is designed as a continuous journey with new moments throughout.

497ace81-156c-4c8b-bf1d-b9d184ec7be6.description:
This design starts from the site's existing conditions and aims to retain vegetation to the greatest extent possible. The building intentionally avoids all trees. And around the trees, courtyard spaces of different sizes are generated. The sloping roof element is inspired by the local traditional architectural elements in Uganda. In the design, the continuous sloping roof can provide sun shading and rain protection for circulation between the different building blocks.

Rainwater captured in the channel between the two roof slopes is directed to the courtyards in the rainy season, where planting helps filter it before it enters an underground cistern. To support deliveries and daily access, the kitchen and multi-functional classroom sit near the road. In the southern hemisphere, north light and preserved trees create shade for the event space and shifting shadows in the courtyards. A playground wraps the site's largest tree at the north end. Interwoven courtyards improve daylight and natural ventilation, while the northwest-facing roof planes host solar panels for greater efficiency.

The building uses common, locally available materials and construction methods suited to local labor skills. Walls are made from mud bricks fired from local soil, allowing community members and students to help produce materials for future school expansions. The roof is corrugated sheet metal supported by a continuous timber truss system, helping keep costs low.

152bf470-3a59-4c51-a2f6-bb37f2b18e34.description:
The new beer spa will be located southeast of the existing Sel-Hótel Mývatn, facing the lake to offer a stunning view. Large openings on the east side will frame this view, with ground-level doors connecting indoor spaces to an expansive outdoor terrace. Public areas, such as the souvenir shop, snack bar, and brewery, will occupy the ground floor for accessibility, while more private spaces, such as treatment rooms and changing areas, will be on the second floor. A third-floor semi-outdoor terrace, sheltered by a pitched roof, will provide a unique year-round experience.

CONSTRUCTION & MATERIALS:
Utilizing a concrete foundation and core, the main structure will feature a timber design, respecting local construction practices. Cross-laminated timber (CLT) will support wide columns, beams, and slabs, while dark or charred wood as cladding will echo the region's earthy tones. Each floor will cantilever on the east side, enhancing the terrace's shelter and interior lighting.

ACCESSIBILITY & CIRCULATION:
Thoughtful design separates visitor flows, distinguishing those visiting for leisure or the brewery from spa guests. Accessibility is prioritized, with a northern elevation facilitating movement across all levels. Staircases strategically placed offer access to different areas, ensuring spa visitors have a dedicated entry to maintain privacy and convenience.

049d9361-4518-4e63-9b71-c14c23c2c678.description:
AGRIBOX reimagines vertical farming as both a high-performance agricultural machine and a cultural landmark for South Los Angeles. Conceived as a modular megastructure, it provides vast column-free interiors by leveraging off-site steel systems from Manni Sipre. These truss-based units maximize spatial flexibility while streamlining fabrication, installation, and long-term scalability.

Wrapped in a high-performance glass envelope, AGRIBOX is divided into three thermally independent climate zones, each served by dedicated AHUs. This system fine-tunes growing environments to specific crops, improving yield and energy efficiency. The inner workings of agriculture are made visible through a spiraling glass walkway that offers controlled public access and a didactic journey from soil to harvest.

A luminous LED matrix embedded in the façade projects dynamic interpretations of crop circles—ancient symbols of cultivation—bridging the agricultural past with a technological future. This digital skin also acts as a low-light beacon during nighttime conditions and wildfire events, addressing contemporary safety needs.

At the top, a rooftop community space—reached by a continuous public spiral stair—invites visitors to rest, learn, and engage with the landscape while observing farming against the skyline. The result is a rare fusion of education, sustainability, and urban leisure.

AGRIBOX is not merely a farm; it is a beacon of future agriculture—an urban infrastructure designed for resilience, transparency, and collective nourishment.
049d9361-4518-4e63-9b71-c14c23c2c678.team: SHIMIN ZHOU, SHIDA WANG, XINLEI GUO

703ddcbe-a47c-4da7-8ad1-f2c8d0153dba.description:
Set between forest canopy and streambed, Rain Gallery curates an immersive encounter with Yakushima's landscape and climate. A charred-wood façade and slender steel columns echo the rhythm of the surrounding tree trunks, anchored by a chunky masonry base. Above, a butterfly roof acts as an instrument of rain and light: it gathers water toward a central skylight–drain, where droplets strike a thin film, ripple outward, and slip into rain chains that deliver water into the grey space between rooms. 

Here, rain becomes the project's spatial organizer—shaping thresholds, tempering air, and making sound and refraction tangible across inside and out. Rustling leaves, the stream below, and raindrops on the roof form a shifting chorus; drifting cloud shadows slide along the long eave and mark time. The house becomes a gallery connecting the mountain and sea by framing changing weather as a daily experience.
703ddcbe-a47c-4da7-8ad1-f2c8d0153dba.team: CHRISSIE CHEN, SHIMIN ZHOU, YIBO LIN, RUOQI JIANG, CHANGSHU CHEN
